text: The gate has been opened. Come in and bring with you as many as you can. This should be your motivation to get up in the morning. Chapter 1/ Seeking an ideal I intend to share here the path that led to my Faith in Jesus Christ as the only way to the Father. As He Himself says: "I am the way and the truth and the life. No one cornes to the Father except through me" (reference). I developed, during my late teen-hood, a very big admiration to Gandhi. He seemed tome as an admirable public figure who has worked tirelessly for his people and their liberation. What made him particularly special to me was that he did that through non- violent means, even accepting to go to prison a dozen times for a combined period of more than 6 years. ("Be the change you want to see in the world" and so many other beautiful of his sayings abound on the internet.) His many fasts for social reconciliation, including his 21 days fast for Hindu-Muslim unity, can't but be greatly admired. Even Albert Einstein said about him after his death: "Generations to corne will scarce believe that such a man as his walked upon this earth". His letter to Hitler pleading to do what he can to avoid World War II is another example of rus inspiring peaceful activism in a world that was then oh how tormented by military tensions. With all that in minci, he was far from being perfect, as he himself acknowledged without hesitation. What I however did, like what people generally do with their idols, is consider him as the ultimate example. In fact, the same word "idol" refers to both an object of worship and adoration as well as one of great admiration. Around that time, I also got acquainted with the work of Mother Teresa of Calcutta and her extraordinary service to the poorest in India, and all over the world. The movie which was released in 2022 "Mother Teresa: no greater love" depicts well the love behind her service to the most marginalized in our global society. Looking at her life, I thought I had found an answer to my existential questionings of late teenhood: "THIS is a life worth living" I said to myself. The Christian Faith was at the center of her life. She once recounted Jesus telling her "My little one - corne - carry Me into the holes of the poor. - Come be My light - I cannot go alone - they don't know Me - in your love for Me - they will see Me, know Me, want Me.... For them I long -Wilt thou refuse?". What impeded my complete imitation of her was reading about the doubts she had about her Faith. She expressed them in many letters, one of which she wrote to a reverend saying "Jesus has a very special love for you. As for me, the silence and the emptiness is so great that I look and do not see, listen and do not hear". These doubts, which were only part of her long and arduous spiritual path, greatly discouraged me at the time. Looking at her as a "figure of authority" and example, I thought that if SHE doubted at some point in her life, then, their must be a problem with the abject of her faith. This made me put the faith aspect aside and continue focusing on a secular approach to humanitarianism. On the same line of humanitarian logic, and through Gandhi, I was introduced ta Lean Tolstoy who had been one of his major influences, especially by means of his book "The Kingdom of Gad is within you". I was deeply amazed by him and his work, reading many of his books and articles. One sentence, found in the last paragraph of the aforementioned book, particularly impacted me by joining the hurnanitarian ideology I had adopted: "The sole meaning of life is ta serve humanity". Tolstoy, being barn and raised in a Christian Orthodox environment as well as an admirer of Christian scripture, had obviously views and opinions on the Christian Faith and on the Church. In spite of his very high esteem of Christ and His teachings, his views of Him excluded His deification. He didn't think of Him as being simultaneously real Gad and real man. He also didn't hold true His miracles, including His Resurrection, rather considering them symbolic. Because I looked at him as an example and an authority, I unfortunately quickly adopted his views. This meant putting Christ in the same category as other historical figures, and "spiritual teachers". Very lamentably, this was everything it took for placing me out of the worship of the real Gad. Chapter 2/ On Civil disobedience and revolution It is worth noting that Tolstoy was deeply inspired by Christ's Sermon on the Mount. This passage condenses Christ's teaching and its novelty, putting it apart from all others. It can't be summarized in a sentence or two as each is full of deep meanings. Everyone who's capable of reading it should do it for himself. Among the most impactful verses are Matthew's 5:38-39: "You have heard that it was said, 'Eye for eye, and tooth for tooth'. But I tell you, do not resist an evil persan. If anyone slaps you on the right cheek, turn ta them the other cheek also." and Matthew's 5:43-45: "You have heard that it was said, 'Love your neighbor and hate your enemy.' But I tell you, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, that you may be children of your Father in heaven. He causes his sun to rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous " Tolstoy adopted an anarchist socio-political interpretation ta the Sermon on the Mount that greatly influenced my political views for a long period of time. It is a position that is held profusely in today's world, especially among the youth. In fact, Tolstoy saw an opposition between the non-violent doctrine of Christ and the very existence of states, which are, indeed, ultimately based on military violence and coercion. To defend his anarchist views, Tolstoy points out that this violence can't but marginalize a portion of, sometimes the majority, of the population in order ta assure the comfort and wellbeing of the remaining. This is actually true for all governments which have ever existed. The haves and haves-not divide has always existed. Jesus confirms that when Mary of Bethany anointed His feet with expensive perfume, Judas exclaimed "Why was this perfume not sold for three hundred denarii and the money given ta the poor?". Jesus then replies by saying "Leave her alone [...] You always have the poor with you, but you do not always have me." The solution proposed by both Gandhi and Tolstoy to such injustices was non-violent civil disobedience. In other words, a rebellious and revolutionary, although non-violent, non- participation in what is deemed unjust. For Gandhi, this meant directly collecting salt from the sea and knitting clothes in order to avoid benefiting the British colonizers through taxes, and ultimately weakening them. More theoretically, but quite drastically, for Tolstoy this meant the abolition of nation states altogether, always through non- participation and non-compliance with their rules. For a long time, I held it as being the good and right solution. I dreamed of self sufficiency, farm living, and autonomous communities: a way of life that would completely withdraw me and those around me from the "imperialist neoclassical" system we live in. After finishing my bachelors, I even worked full-time for four months on an organic farm with the intention of eventually moving towards a more local and self- sufficient lifestyle. Aside from the impracticality of the endeavor, especially if it is to be applied on a large scale, at some point I realized that civil disobedience is not as Christian as I had thought. The image of Christ carying Himself His Cross on the Road to Cavalry, where he was to be crucified, made me realize that ultimate non-resistance to evil entails conforming toits demands when it is in position of authority. Otherwise, in such cases, disobedience only creates further tension. This is well demonstrated in the scene between Jesus and Pontius Pilate, the roman officer who ordered the execution of Jesus. Here is the passage from John 19:9-11 : "Where do you corne from?" he [Pontius Pilate] asked Jesus, but Jesus gave him no answer. "Do you refuse to speak tome?" Pilate said. "Don't you realize I have power either to free you or to crucify you?" Jesus answered, "You would have no power over me if it were not given to you from above." Jesus' answer then legitimizes Pilate's earthly authority over Him. In other words, this authority, which "cornes from above", is part of God's scheme and, hence, needs to be obeyed. Rather than negating governmental authority, Jesus' teachings include it. The same dynamic can be found in other situations that put together two persans, one having authority over the other: a child and a parent, a student and a teacher, a boss and an employee, or a superior in a monastery and a monk. This legitimization of authority gives place to the virtues of respect, submission, and obedience to those higher in the hierarchy of authority, a virtue that has been greatly lost in today's occidental culture lacking direction. Ultimately, Jesus accepts to submit to the earthly authority of Pontius Pilate in order to perfectly obey the Absolute authority, which cames from God. In fact, the night before His trial, Jesus repeatedly prayed, with great fervor, the Heavenly Father that this accusation which awaits him be taken out "My Father, if it is possible, may this cup be taken from me". He then voices His total submission to the Will of God by saying "Yet not as I will, but as you will." (Matthew 26:39). God's Will was then Jesus' infinitely humble submission to earthly rulers. This was the price of redemption of humankind. In fact, He told Peter who tried to defend Him from arrest with a sword: "Put your sword back in its place [...] "Do you think I cannot call on my Father, and he will at once put at my disposa! more than twelve legions of angels? But how then would the Scriptures be fulfilled that say it must happen in this way?" (Matthew 26:52-54). In John 10:18, Jesus says "No one takes it (His life) from me, but Ilay it down of rny own accord". To confirm Jesus' position on authority, He was asked on another occasion whether His interlocutors should pay their taxes. He answered by asking to see a money coin and then interrogating them on the image and inscription on it. After hearing their answer, which was "Caesar's", Jesus said "Give back to Caesar what is Caesar's and to God what is God's". This implies that we have responsibilities to both earthly rulers and to God, and hence that denying any of the two is problematic. There is then a notable distinction between what Gandhi and Tolstoy proned as the ultimate solution to injustice and the doctrine of Christ. The first, although labeled "non- violent", contains a component of resistance. It aims to negate an existing and established authority through non-participation in it. Ultimately, it is a form of confrontation, which will then eventually lead to defeat. In fact, can it be posited that India gained more "independence" because of Gandhi's campaigns? Or is it more accurate to say that 1) After WW2, India's independence happened around the same time as that of many other countries and 2) Colonialism was in fact replaced by a more colonial system after WW21 namely neocolonialism. Christ's approach goes further in non-resistance to evil as it seeks to accept and absorb all of it as in "If anyone slaps you on the right cheek, turn to them the other cheek also". Building on the premise that resistance to evil only accentuates it ("all who draw the sword will die by the sword" Matthew 26:52), Christ's approach is wiser and aims for complete pacificism. Adopting the first imparted a rebellious and very critical spirit that stayed in me for a long time. It created a chronic interna! tension that deprived me of much inner peace all along. I gradually came to realize the futility and counter-productivity of resisting, even "non-violently", that which one seeks to change. It's wasted energy that actually makes the overall outcome worse. I realized I wasn't making the world a better place, all I was doing is feeling defeated and growing in bitterness. When possible, energy is well used either to suggest a different path to authority, denounce its current path, or by embodying and working on the alternative with the resources and possibilities at hand, always without going against it. In a lot of cases, much good can be done within the constraints of authority. In Catholic terms, this most often applies to all the "works of mercy", both the 7 corporal (feeding the hungry, giving water to the thirsty, clothing the naked, sheltering the homeless, visiting the sick, visiting the imprisoned, or ransoming the captive, and burying the dead), and the 7 spiritual (instructing the ignorant, counseling the doubtful, admonishing the sinners, bearing patiently those who wrong us, forgiving offenses, comforting the afflicted, and praying for the living and the dead.) How much good can for instance be done if only the wealthy gave a portion of what they have to the poor? Jesus gives much importance to these acts by saying "whatever you did for one of the least of these brethren of mine, you did for me." (Matthew 25:40). However, as the ultimate Kingdom is His, the Sons of God are destined to be in collision with earthly authority. When that happens, the best and wisest approach is to sacredly submit to it, as a God given, and sacrificially accept the detrimental consequences. This has been repeatedly foreseen by Jesus, among other in Matthew 10:16 "See, I am sending you out like sheep into the midst of wolves", and in Luke 14:27 "Whoever does not carry the cross and follow me cannot be my disciple". The history of the Church is in fact built on the blood of oh how many martyrs starting with Christ himself, and then all of His 12 disciples, all dying as martyrs with the exception of John. This has been Jesus' way of doing throughout His Life: first doing all the good He could, then defending Himself against accusations, which included vigorously denouncing His accusers (see, among other, the 7 woes He addresses to the scripts and pharisees in Matthew 23), then finally sacredly submitting to them and to authority through silence and prayer to the Heavenly Father. Matthew 27:12 says "But when the leading priests and the elders made their accusations against him, Jesus remained silent." In the case of an oppressive and unjust authority, the Christian path to change is to happen through individual, and not systemic, conversion. The perfect example is that of the conversion of the roman soldier Longinus, later Saint Longinus, who pierced Jesus' side while on the cross to make sure He was dead and subsequently exclaimed "Surely this man was the Son of Gad!" (Mark 15:39) The ultimate triumph of good and justice over evil and oppression is to happen at Christ's Resurrection, three days after His death. Him being the "first-born", as scripture repeatedly describes Him, paves the way for all of us in His Kingdom, the Kingdom of the justs. Chapter 3/ The case of the Jewish nation It is very interesting to note that the accusations against Jesus on the day of His trial came from religious, and not political authority. It is the Jewish "leading priests and the elders" who made them, not the roman officer, Pontius Pilate who found "no case against him." Oohn 19:4). He, however, ended up condemning Him to death because of pressure from the Jewish people: his main fear being aJewish revolt taking place within the Roman empire if he weren't to concede to their rage and demand. It is then worth asking why the leading Jews were against Him. To put in context, with the belief in Gad the Creator, the awaited coming of the Messiah, the Son of Gad, represents the other founding premise of Judaism. Descriptions and prophecies about His future coming abound in Jewish scriptures. Accepting that the Messiah has corne implies that the old era has ended and a new one has started. The old era and the waiting are represented by Judaism, and Jewish priests, eiders, and institutions. In short, when the waiting ends, there would no longer be place for them. Oxymoronically, the Messiah represents then a threat to the Jewish nation. In Mathew 5:17, Jesus says "Do not think that I have corne to abolish the law or the prophets (of Judaism); I have corne not to abolish but to fulfill." In conformity with the previous description, Judaism and Christianity are then not to be seen as two separate religions, but as one: one being the fulfillment of the other. Note that the Jewish people were Jesus' priority throughout His ministry. When Jesus sent out His disciples to announce that the Messiah had corne, and that He was Him, He made sure that they start with Jewish towns and villages by saying "Do not go among the Gentiles or enter any town of the Samaritans. Go rather to the lost sheep of Israel." (Mathew 10:5-6). Also, before accepting to heal the daughter of the insistent Canaanite woman, Jesus told her "I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel." (Mathew 15:21-28). With the increasingly undeniable signs thatJesus accomplished painting out that He was the awaited Messiah, culminating in the raising from the dead of Lazaraus four days after his death Uohn 11: 1-44), the vast majority of the little Jewish people believed in Him. Expectedly, this made Jewish leaders worry. John 11:47-48 says "So the chief priests and the Pharisees called a meeting of the council, and said, "What are we to do? This man Uesus] is performing many signs. If we let him go on like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will corne and destroy both our holy place and our nation." The siding of the little people with Jesus is clearly demonstrated on Palm Sunday, only five days before Jesus' trial, when He made His entry to Jerusalem with the triumphal acclamation of the people shouting "Hosanna! Blessed is the one who cornes in the name of the Lord-the King of Israel!" Uohn 12:13). Unsurprisingly, this made high-placed Jews worry even further and say "You see, you can do nothing. Look, the world has gène after him!" Uohn 12:19). In the five days leading to Jesus' trial, which happened the next Friday, Jewish authorities succeeded in convincing enough of the Jewish people to side against Him and actually demand His death by crucifixion. The main argument is that of the high priest Caiaphas: "You do not understand that it is better for you to have one man die for the people than to have the whole nation destroyed." Uohn 12:49-50). Quite tragically, the shouting of the people went from "Hosanna! Blessed is the one who cornes in the name of the Lord-the King of Israel!" in John 12:13 on Palm Sunday to "Crucify him! Crucify him!" (Luke 23:21) five days later on Good Friday. In fact, with the exception of a few, those who believed in Him preferred their security over the Truth. Out of fear, they deserted and denied Him. With the exception of the beloved disciple John, ten of the twelve disciples, the closest persans to Him, deserted and denied Him, at the example of Peter who denied Him trice before sunrise (Luke 22:54-62). Judas Iscariot, the twelfth disciple actually betrayed Him and handed Him to authority in exchange for a sum of money. The tragedy here is that Jesus' miracles, which testified that He was the Messiah, and which were accomplished out of love and compassion for the sick and the dying, very mainly among the Jews, are what led Him to His death on the cross, demanded by the very same people; the people He had chosen. Chapter 4/ Vegetarianism, the act of killing In the absence of an ultimate figure and example of Good and Truth, and even with the most hurnanistic intentions, all sorts of ideologies and ideals can't but emerge. In my case, it was first moral vegetarianism which is the abstinence from meat-eating with the aim of avoiding the killing of animals. It is in fact very painful, disturbing, and confusing to see an animal being killed by another, or slaughtered for food or other purposes by a human being. The scene of a lion preying upon and devouring a gazelle can't but feel horrendous and sorrowful. Seeing a sheep butchered as part of a sacrificial ceremony in Aleppo was the reason for which I first became vegetarian. In a Utopian world, humans won't need to eat animals and animals won't have to prey on each other. In the story of the book of Genesis, after God created man, He declared: "I give you every seed-bearing plant on the face of the whole earth and every tree that has fruit with seed in it. They will be yours for food." This account describes the original human diet foreseen by God: it is in short a fruitarian one. In the same line of logic, Isaiah 65:25 says: "The wolf and the young lamb will feed together, the lion will eat hay like the ox, and dust be the serpent's food. No hurt, no harm will be done on all my holy mountain, Yahweh says." The fruitarian diet for humans makes sense from a perspective of non-harm. In fact, if one is to avoid all harm demands being more than vegetarian, even vegan. In fact, it is easy to agree that milk and egg production cause suffering and death to animals. Mammals produce milk for their offsprings and the intention of egg laying is to procreate. At the detriment of animals, humans intervene in the process to draw nutrition. In the case of eggs, male chicks are eliminated as soon as possible as they are not necessary for production. Females are also eliminated when they can no longer lay eggs adequately. In the case of milk, calves are taken from their mothers and killed in order for humans to take the milk. However, eating vegetables (leaves, roots, etc) and grains also causes harm. It either degrades the organism or even kills it. Of course, vegetables don't have a neurological system that resembles ours, like animals do. That however doesn't mean that they don't get harmed or that they don't suffer. This makes only the consumption of fruits harm-free. Trees, in fact, give their fruits completely voluntarily, laying them on the ground, in offering, when ripe. After a year of vegetarianism and nearly five of veganism, and in spite of all my vigorous efforts to eat as healthy as possible and meet all dietary recommendations, I had, like many other, at some point to re-include some animal products, like fish, into my diet. My energy level as well as my strength were diminishing. I also developed very unpleasant and persistent digestive issues. The ideal of non-harm however stayed in my psyche as true and desirable. For this reason, but mostly in an attempt to remedy to the health problems I was dealing with, I became, a few years later, a proponent of frugivorism. I practiced it to the best of my abilities for around two years thinking it was the right way to go and that the reason of my bad past experience with veganism simply needed correction. Instead of solving my health problems, and because of many important deficiencies of proteins, fats, and minerals, this unfortunately greatly aggravated them. By continuing to read the book of Genesis, one sees that the situation changed after a very important event: The Fall of Man. It is the event that marks the exile of Man from the Garden of Eden, in other words; Paradise, which is the living in complete accordance with the Will of the Creator. This happened after God had ordained Man to eat from all fruits except one by saying "You may eat indeed of all the trees in the garden. Nevertheless of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you are not to eat, for on the day you eat of it you shall most surely die." Genesis 2:16-17 As many know the rest of the story, and after being tempted by the the spirit of evil acting by means of the snake, Man is to disobey God's commandment and eat of the forbidden fruit. In consequence, Man lost his innocence. Having eaten from the "tree of knowledge of good and evil", he could now differentiate between them, and consequently consciously choose the latter; something he increasingly did. This came at his detriment for sure, first by making him mortal as the verse says, but then at the price of increasing disorder and suffering as the rest of Genesis, and the following books describe. Given the important place of Man in God's creation, his fall not only marks the beginning of disorder in his affairs, but also in those of all creation. According to the book of Genesis, this is when God changes Man's diet by saying "Every moving thing that lives shall be food for you; and just as I gave you the green plants, I give you everything" Genesis 9:3-4 In other words, the introduction of harm through the killing of other creatures for food was a consequence of the Fall, man's departure from God. This makes seeking to address the harm itself, without passing through its cause, ultimately futile. In fact, it is even sinful in that it aims to erase and contradict the divine sequence of events. Christ's teachings go in that direction. In Marc 7:15-23, He clearly proclaims "Nothing that goes into someone from outside can make that person unclean; it is the things that corne out of someone that make that person unclean" Then speaking to His disciples who were having difficulty understanding, He said "Can't you see that nothing that goes into someone from outside can make that person unclean, because it goes not into the heart but into the stomach and passes into the sewer? And he went on, 'lt is what cornes out of someone that makes that person unclean. For it is from within, from the heart, that evil intentions emerge: fornication, theft, murder, adultery, avarice, malice, deceit, indecency, envy, slander, pride, folly. All these evil things corne from within and make a person unclean." Chapter 5/ Linking interior and exterior harm In genesis 2:17, it is said that Man is to die after eating from the forbidden fruit. "Nevertheless of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you are not to eat, for on the day you eat of it you shall most surely die." This means that man was immortal before disobeying God's command. Illness and death are then a result of man's fall, of sin. The disease cornes from the exile. Just like a plant which has its roots eut withers and eventually dies soit is when we are disconnected from God, our Source. In short, spiritual illness cornes first andsubsequently manifests itself in physical and mental illnesses. It is the reason why when Jesus heals a person, He first forgives him his sins. An example of that is the healing of the paralytic. Luke's account (5:18-26) goes as follows: And behold, some men were bringing on a bed a man who was paralyzed, and they were seeking to bring him in and lay him before Jesus, but finding no way to bring him in, because of the crowd, they went up on the roof and let hirn down with his bed through the tiles into the midst before Jesus. And when he saw their faith, he said, "Man, your sins are forgiven." And the scribes and the Pharisees began to question, saying, "Who is this who speaks blasphemies? Who can forgive sins but God alone?" When Jesus perceived their thoughts, he answered them, "Why do you question in your hearts? Which is easier, to say, 'Your sins are forgiven you,' or to say, 'Rise and walk'? But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins"-he said to the man who was paralyzed-"I say to you, rise, pick up your bed and go home." And immediately he rose up before them and picked up what he had been lying on and went home, glorifying God." This passage, among others, demonstrates the parallel between physical healing and the forgiveness of sins. When it is sin that's causing the disease, it becomes futile to seek to address the illness while staying in it. Like the example of the paralytic, being forgiven and redeemed by the Almighty are then needed. Linking this with the previous findings on harm, we can see that there is a direct link between the external and internal disorder resulting from Man's departure from the Will of God. Man's departure from the Will of God causes both internal and external, or environmental, harm. This allows us to see the important and unique role that humans have among all other species in that they are alone capable of having a disordering impact on creation at large. This is very clearly seen in today's ecological crisis. What other creature is capable of having such an impact on creation itself? None. This capacity that we alone have, and which differentiates us from animals, cornes _from what made sin possible from the first place: our aptitude to differentiate good from evil, and chose between them. Animals certainly have a capacity for care and altruism however, they won't exhibit feelings of guilt, remorse, or shame when "acting wrongly" in the wild as there's no right and wrong from the first place. Trained animals or pets can express feelings of guilt or remorse but only towards their human masters, not towards the Absolute, (and out of fear of rejection, not love.) This is not to say that sin is the cause of all diseases. Sorne have divine motives. This was the subject of interrogation among Christ's disciples when wondering about the reason a persan was born blind. Here is the passage in John 9:1-3 As he went along, he Uesus] saw a man blind from birth. His disciples asked him, "Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?". "Neither this man nor his parents sinned," said Jesus, "but this happened so that the works of God might be displayed in him. In this case, the "works of God" was Jesus healing him so that people may believe that He is the awaited Son of God. God's works and motives are of course persona! to each. Going back to the case where sin is the cause of the disease, and just like the external harm cannot be dealt with without addressing its root (the Fall), the internal harm, or the disease can't as well. Jesus' teachings go in this direction when he says "Nothing that goes into someone from outside can make that person unclean; it is the things that corne out of someone that make that persan unclean". Chapter 6/ Harmful and poisonous ingredients This doesn't mean that there is no harmful or poisonous ingredients capable of disturbing the natural functioning of an organism or a human being. They abound ranging from germs, to artificial chemical compounds, tobacco, poisons, certain drugs, heavy metals, etc. Certain are less harmful but still are like sugar, alcohol, and over-processed foods. These can enter a human body either through the action of the individual himself (like by smoking tobacco), through the actions of other humans (like breathing polluted air, or second hand smoking), or through other creatures (like being bitten by a snake or catching a virus). In the first two cases, it can be done consciously or unconsciously. In all cases, however, the harm takes root in the departure from the will of God. Starting with the first case, when smoking tobacco for example, or smoking anything else on that matter, one can ask: what human need was sought to be met when the first humans endeavored to roll some leaves together, burn them, put them in their mouth, and inhale the smoke? Clearly, there's something distorted in the endeavor. It took centuries, even millenia, for science to make a link between smoking and health problems. Not to say that it's not important, quite the contrary, what science actually did is confirm that there was a distortion in the matter. When smoking became socially accepted, even encouraged thanks to tobacco companies which sought to link it with status and prestige, the harm inflicted by smoking became both self and socially-inflicted. The social component is more prominent in other cases like that of second hand smoking, breathing polluted city air, or eating over-processed food marketed for monetary motives. This is where the concept of ecological sin cornes in. It was described at the conclusion of the Vatican's synod of bishops on the Amazon in the following way: "We propose to define ecological sin as an action or omission against Gad, against one's neighbor, the community and the environment. It is sin against future generations, and it is committed in acts and habits of pollution and destruction of the harmony of the environment. These are transgressions against the principles of interdependence, and they destroy networks of solidarity among creatures and violate the virtue of justice." Finally, the harm or the poisonous ingredient can corne from the natural environment or from other creatures. The most symbolic example is that of the serpent and its highly poisonous venom. In the 3rd chapter of the Book of Genesis, when God discovers that His two newly created human beings, Adam and Eve, disobeyed His command of not eating from the fruit of the tree of knowledge of good and evil, the first creature He punishes is the serpent that fooled them into believing that no consequence is to arise from their consumption ("But the serpent said to the woman, "You will not die; for Gad knows that when you eat of it your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil." Genesis 3:4-5). God then cursed and punished the serpent by saying "I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and hers; he will strike your head, and you will strike his heel." (Genesis 3:14). As man has transgressed his union with the Creator, a schism was created not only between him and Gad, but also, as explained before, between him and the natural environment, as represented by the serpent, and with which he is going to have a mutually conflictual relationship. Following the same logic disharmony, after the Fall, God said to Adam "cursed is the ground because of you; in toil you shall eat of it all the days of your life; thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you" (Genesis 3:17- 18). The schism between Man and God, Man and himself, Man and his neighbor, and Man and the natural environment were also accompanied by a schism between man and woman. Before the Fall, Adam and Eve were nude with each other in Eden. This represents the reign of complete confidence between them. It is when they ate of the fruit of the tree of knowledge that "the eyes of both were opened" (Genesis 3:7) and they "knew they were naked" (idem). This is when separation started taking place between them as represented by them "[sewing] fig leaves together and [making] loincloths for themselves" (idem). All this to say that whether the harmful or poisonous substance enters the human body through one's, other's, or natural actions, the harm itself takes its roots from the event of the Fall and the schisms it has engendered, before which Man was immortal and no possibility for harm existed. The coming of Christ the Redeemer and the Reconciler paves the way for this perfect harmony to take place again. Now, we are not talking about abstract ideas, but The Truth. About That which is in perfect alignment with what is True. That's why intelligence can and should be a facilitator to Faith in Gad. It is easy to agree that believing what is not true to be true doesn't make it as such. In fact, in the case of a psychotic persan, it is very widely accepted that the sooner health practitioners intervene and help, the higher his or her chances of resuming a normal life. Otherwise, because of the widening gap as time goes on between what is true and what the patient holds as such, untreated psychotic persans are at a very high risk of becoming homeless and even committing suicide. Being aligned with the Truth and seeking It, at the expense of everything going against It, is what anyone can and should do to move forward. Revelation 3:20 Appendix 1: Conversion to Catholicism After more than five years of spiritual pursuit that led me to many traditions as well as the so called "new age spirituality" (which I now regard as demonic), I profess my faith in Jesus Christ, and my belief that salvation can only be attained through Him. As a reminder, salvation is why and what we are here for. It is not about wealth accumulation, pleasures, experiences, procreation, or "assuring one's future". This can't be assured my friends. Not even one milli-second of it. Salvation is about total denial of oneself, and one's plans, and total surrender to the Plan of God. Since we are so away from that, and our ego is so dear, we needed grace to save us. We needed to be re-included and forgiven by the Creator in spite of our arrogance and transgressions. This is why Jesus Christ, who is God's manifestation in human form, came to Earth: to tell us that we are forgiven, and that we belong no matter what. Why do I say thatJesus Christ is God's manifestation in human form, or "The Son of God"? Based on the writings, ask this question: Who actually transcended the world? Who is from beyond the World? (i.e from the Creator) Who fed the people? Who challenged gravity? Who returned sight to the blind? Who gave back life to the dead? Who remained loving in spite of the whole world's ignorance? Who rose from the dead? Who transcended time? Who is it other than Jesus Christ? Once we recognize the Deity of Jesus Christ, we see that "He is in the Father, and the Father is in Him": God acts and speaks through Him. So when Jesus forgives the worst transgression ever committed in human history while dying on the cross by saying "Father, forgive them, for they don't know what they are doing." (Luke 23:34), it is God forgiving the totality of humanity's transgressions ever committed, and ever to be committed. What a love and what a joy. We have been forgiven by the Creator. All it takes is to accept this forgiveness.
